nameStory: Meadow hawkweed gets its name from growing in open meadows and fields, while the "hawkweed" part comes from an old belief that hawks ate these plants to sharpen their eyesight. Its many colorful nicknames like "devil's paintbrush" and "king devil" reflect how this bright yellow wildflower can spread aggressively and take over areas where it's not wanted.
description: Meadow hawkweed is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms dense patches in open areas. It produces bright yellow, dandelion-like flowers on thin stems that rise 1-3 feet above a flat rosette of fuzzy leaves. The plant spreads both by seeds and underground runners called stolons, often creating carpets of cheerful yellow blooms in summer meadows and fields.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow composite flowers about 1 inch across, very similar to dandelions but held on thin, leafless stems well above the ground. Each flower head is made up of many small ray petals (like tiny yellow tongues) with no central disk.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: All leaves form a flat rosette at ground level, never growing up the flower stems. Leaves are spoon-shaped to oval, soft and fuzzy to the touch, with a grayish-green color from dense white hairs covering both surfaces.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading patches through underground runners. The leafy rosettes stay flat against the ground while only the thin flower stems reach upward, creating a distinctive two-layer appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are thin, wiry, and completely leafless, rising 1-3 feet above the basal rosette. Stems feel slightly rough and are covered with small hairs that you can see when backlit by sunlight.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy white seed heads similar to dandelions, but smaller and held higher off the ground on those distinctive leafless stems. Seeds have white, feathery parachutes for wind dispersal.

habitat: Look for meadow hawkweed in open, sunny areas like fields, meadows, pastures, and roadsides throughout New England. It thrives in poor to moderately fertile soils and can tolerate both acidic and neutral conditions. This adaptable plant often establishes in disturbed areas and gradually spreads to form large colonies in grasslands.

seasonality.spring: Fuzzy gray-green leaf rosettes emerge early and remain flat against the ground. No flowers yet, but the distinctive hairy leaves in neat circular patterns are visible in open areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with bright yellow flowers from June through August. This is when the plant is most easily spotted and identified, with leafless flower stems rising well above the ground-hugging foliage.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and fluffy seed heads appear, dispersing in late summer and fall. Basal leaves remain green and continue photosynthesis as the plant stores energy in its roots for next year.
seasonality.winter: Leaves die back completely, leaving only the root system and underground runners alive. Look for dried, brown flower stems that may persist, marking where colonies grew the previous year.

funFact: Despite being called "devil's paintbrush," meadow hawkweed was once considered so valuable that medieval herbalists believed it could grant hawks supernatural vision - and some people actually tried eating it to improve their own eyesight!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with dandelions, but meadow hawkweed's flowers are held much higher on thin, leafless stems while dandelion flowers sit close to the ground on hollow stems with leaves scattered up the stem. Memory trick: "Hawkweed holds high, dandelions stay down low."
contextualKnowledge: This European native is considered invasive in many parts of New England, where it can outcompete native wildflowers and grasses. While beautiful, it's often unwelcome in agricultural areas because livestock generally won't eat its hairy, bitter-tasting leaves, and it can quickly dominate pastures.
compareHints: Meadow hawkweed differs from its orange hawkweed cousin by having yellow flowers instead of orange-red ones. Compared to mouse-eared hawkweed, meadow hawkweed is taller with more upright flower stems and forms larger, more aggressive colonies. Unlike smooth hawkweed, this species has distinctly fuzzy, hairy leaves that feel soft and velvety to the touch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orange hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctive orange-red flowers—most other hawkweeds in New England have yellow blooms.
Mouse-eared hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctively fuzzy, silvery leaves and single yellow flowers on leafless stems.
Smooth hawkweed towers above its mouse-eared hawkweed cousin, which stays close to the ground in creeping mats with densely fuzzy leaves.
Yellow-devil differs from orange hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and generally paler, more silvery-fuzzy leaves.
Yellow Devil differs from Orange Hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and more tightly clustered flower heads.
